Tape I 11/16/82
Tape II 11/23/82
Where do you want to start?

Well, we have to start at the beginning, I guess. There's a couple of things that they really specifically want to get into, but that's later in your career. But I think we should just begin at the beginning and just go through it.
The beginning of the musical part of my life?
No, your whole life.
Oh, my whole life..
Yeah. You were born in Oklahoma.

Right...and that's about it. [LAUGHS] No, I was born in Oklahoma, but my folks moved to Detroit, you know, when I was really young. In fact, my mother died in Detroit, because... See, she was only there for about a year before she died, so I didn't really get to know her. Then they decided to send me down to my grandmother and live back in Oklahoma -- Haskell, Oklahoma. So I went back down there...
Well, how old were you then?

Oh, about one year old. So I really didn't know my mother, you know. And my father had...he was working in a plant up in Michigan, so he decided to come back down to Oklahoma, and he came down there -- and he died
McGhee (11/16) - 2
when I was five.
So you didn't know him too well either.

Yeah, I didn't know him at all. I know that he had invested some money in a grocery store in Bristow, Oklahoma, and my other uncle had taken that over. After he got sick, he took it over and he started running it. And he left it to me, but I never saw a trace of it. When I went to Bristow, he asked me..."I guess you want to put me through school," and school was the last thing I was thinking of at that time, because...
How old were you then?
Well, I was maybe about twelve, twelve or thirteen, something like that.

Anyway, I wanted to play music, because my brother... I had three half-brothers, all of them played music. One of them was Ben Johnson, he was a bass guitar and piano player. My older brother, Joe, was a pianist, and my younger brother, Cesar Johnson, was a guitarist. So they were all that I knew about, you know. So I was thinking about really playing music. And that's how I got into it. So I after I went up to Bristow and so forth, and...
From Haskell.
Yeah. Well, my grandmother lived in Haskell, see. That's who my mother wanted to take care of
McGhee (11/16) - 3

me. So she took me, took me under her wing. Then we moved up to Sapulpa, Oklahoma, and Grandfather was... He could speak seven dialects of English-Indian languages. So they used to come get him all the time and take him for weekends, and it practically left me with just my grandmother.
He used to go on jobs doing interpreting?
Yeah, he would go and preach in the Indian language. That's the only way he made his money.
Well, what kind of Indians were there? There were Choctaws there?
Well, there was Creek, Choctaw, Seminole, whatever branch it was... He knew all the dialects anyway.

So anyway, he came back home, and I guess I was a bad boy, because I didn't really stay home and do like my grandmother wanted me to. But at that time I was more interested in music. So I used to go out on ...(?). That's how I got to know Frank Wess and Marshall and Ernie Royal.
You knew them way back then.
In Sapulpa, yeah. So he went and put me in a training school down in Boley, Oklahoma.
Boley?
Yeah. And they had a music teacher there. He taught me how to finger the trumpet.
McGhee (11/16) - 4
What had you been playing before the trumpet?
Oh, I just liked music. I wasn't playing anything.
Oh, you hadn't tried anything then.
I hadn't tried any instrument at all.
So the trumpet was your first...

Yeah. Well, I had heard Louis Armstrong, you know, and I figured, 'Well, hell, that's what I want to play. I want to be like Pops,' you know. But when they got the instruments for the school band, the cat, George Buford, who was my music teacher, he had taught me the scale on the trumpet...
Let's get his name again?

George Buford. He had taught me how to play the scale on his trumpet, you know. So I figured he was going to put me on trumpet because I knew the scale, you know. And boy, I was so disappointed, and I was mad like a wet hen. I called him everything under the sun -- underneath my breath, of course. But he put me... He started me out on clarinet, you know. And that made me... You know, that kind of threw me a curve, because I wasn't expecting to play clarinet. I loved trumpet.
But I went on and learned it anyway, you know, because he said, 'Well, either you play this or you don't play.' So
McGhee (11/16) - 5

he knew that I wanted to play, so he just... He shoved me right into it. But I'm glad he did, because at that time, I didn't know nothin'. I didn't know that the clarinet played twice as fast as the trumpet. I didn't have the slightest idea about that, you know. So I'd say, 'Well, okay, if that's what I have to do, this is what I have to do.' So I learned to play the clarinet.

After that, after I really got good on the clarinet, I liked it. I liked the instrument. They had two of us playing clarinet, a guy named Marlin(?) and myself. And I was the best clarinettist out of the two of us. So I figured it was time for me to move and, you know, get to know music. So I decided to split, which I did. I cut out and went to...
This is from Boley.
Yeah. I left Boley and went to Muskogee, Oklahoma.
How old were you then?
Oh, about twelve or thirteen, somewhere along there.

Anyway, I went down to my brother's, my older brother's, and I went to his house. And he said, 'Well, look, there's a possibility I might be able to get you a job with a carnival coming up here pretty soon.' I said, 'Well,
McGhee (11/16) - 6

okay." I said, "I don't know no music, though." So he said, "Well, I'll teach you what you need to know." So he taught me, like, "Dinah" and "Sweet Sue" and numbers like that, something easy that I could play.
And we went on this carnival, and we went up to...we went back to Bristow. I had learned how to play the trumpet, you know, enough to do the tunes at least.
This is on the trumpet.
Yeah. I was back on trumpet, learning.
Oh, I see. I misunderstood. I thought you were still playing the clarinet.
No-no.
Oh, you gave up the clarinet.
I gave up the clarinet and went back to trumpet. That's where I learned how to play "Sweet Sue" and "Sweet Georgia Brown" and so forth.

But then, after that, the gig... They were going further on up into Kansas, and I didn't know nothing about Kansas. So my brother told me, he said, "Let's go back to Muskogee." So I went back down there, and there wasn't no music happening down there, so I figured I'd better make tracks. So I went to Oklahoma City, where my other uncle, my father's sister lived, and I figured, well, maybe I could go there and stay there. And they had more music coming
McGhee (11/16) - 7
through there, because they had the Blue Devils come through there, and Count Basie and all the guys were coming through. So I figured maybe I'd learn more there than I would anywhere else.
Now, when you knew Frank Wess and the Royal Brothers in Sapulpa...
They weren't playing then
They weren't playing, huh?
No, they weren't playing then.
Where did you know them? Just around, huh?
Just from going to school, yeah.
Going to school.
Yeah, going to school. But I mean, Frank and I, we've been friends all since that time. But Marshall and I never did get along too good, because he was older than I was, and I...
I guess he was older than everyone!
[LOUD LAUGHTER]
He was always older!

Yeah! Ha-ha-ha. Yeah, I'm going to tell him you said that. But he was; he was older. Ernie got along and Frank Wess and I got along, but Marshall and I didn't seem to hit it off, for some strange reason.
So, like I was saying, I went to Oklahoma City and I
McGhee (11/16) - 8

got to find out what was happening, and I got discouraged there. I figured I'd go to California to see what was happening. So I got on a train, and me and another cat named Hill, Frank Hill I think his name was, we got on a...hoboed on a train to go to California. And the train stopped right outside of Amarillo [SOUNDS LIKE 'Camarillo.'] And the brakeman saw us on the train and put us off, you know. He said, "You ain't got no business being on this," you know, so forth and so on. Anyway, we...
How old were you then?
Oh, I was just about... Still young.
Still young.
Yeah. Maybe fourteen or fifteen, somewhere around there.
Little did you realize what Camarillo was going to mean later on with Bird.

Yeah. Well, at that time I didn't know they had a Camarillo! I was thinking about going to California. I just wanted to be in California, you know, because I heard that it was pretty good out there, and they had a lot of music going on out there, and they were making pictures and so forth.
Now, Hill was a musician also?
Andrew, no, he was no Hill... Uh, Hill, he
McGhee (11/16) - 9
wasn't a musician, no. But he wanted to go to California, so I figured here's a buddy to run with. But they put us off the train anyway, right outside of Amarillo, Texas.
Oh, Amarillo.
Yeah.
Oh, I thought you had said Camarillo in California.

No-no. Amarillo, Texas. And luckily, we caught a train coming back into Amarillo, so I got that. And I found out my sister was there in town! So I went and found her, and she fed us both and she had my clothes cleaned and pressed, and so forth, so I'd look halfway decent. And I told her I could play the trumpet. And by that time..> They were having a dance that same night anyway. So she said, 'Good. I can take you down there and if you can play some, the guy will let you play, and I can hear what you sound like.'
So I went down and tried to play. I didn't know my ass from a hole in the ground, frankly speaking, to let you know where I was at! Anyway...
You got to start some place.
Everybody has to start some way, so I figured I might as well do that.
So in the meantime, after that was over... Actually, I made a big flop there, because she said, 'No-o, I don't

think so." She didn't think I had played so good, which I didn't, because I didn't know what I was doing anyway. I was just trying, you know! And I got a job around there trying to shine shoes and shit, but I never liked that -- I just couldn't see shining no goddamn shoes.
So we finally got a guy to take us back to Oklahoma City, my sister and I. So we went to Oklahoma City. And I run into Henry Bridges. Have you ever heard of him?
Yeah, the tenor player.

Yeah, a tenor player. Well, actually, I got to know him. And he was working with a quartet out there at some drive-in place where the people would drive in and they'd request numbers. He'd play a number for them, and then, you know, you'd take the hat around and they'd go and throw tips in it and so forth. So he said, "Why don't you come and take up the money?" and so forth. But I really wanted to play. So I'd say, "Well, look, how about letting me play, too?" He said, "Well, that's all right. When we ain't got nothin' to do, I'll teach you what I know." So he taught me a lot of songs that I had never heard of.

But anyway, we did that for a while, and I got so I could eat by taking up the change, and the guys would chip in and give me something to have so I could go to a restaurant, after we got back in town, and eat, and so forth

and so on.
So a guy came in town named Bill Powell -- he was a singer and dancer.
Bill Powell?

Yeah. Bill Powell. And he came in, and Henry told him about me, that I was a trumpet player. So he asked me would I want to go down to Seminole, Oklahoma. So I said, 'Why not? I ain't workin' here. I ain't makin' no money anyway.'
Now, where were you living at this time?
Oh, I was living in Oklahoma City at some place that I had rented from a lady for three dollars a week. A horrible place...
Just a place...
Just a place to be, just to sleep.
Anyway, so he decided to take me down to Seminole. And I ran into a guy named Rotherie Reeves, who was a piano player; he played that old-time piano.
Rotherie?
Yeah, Rotherie.
That's an unusual name.
Yeah. Well, he was an unusual fellow, because he played that old-time music. I didn't like it, but I had to learn it because he was the only one I could
play with. And like I say, Bill Powell was the leader of the thing...
And the singer.

Yeah. We played in this restaurant. I learned a lot of music there, because I had a chance to practice every day and play at night. And when you can do that, you can learn, whether you want to or not, because they call lots of different numbers, and if Rotherie could play it, I could play it, because I'd just watch him and see how he played it -- and I'd play it.

So that lasted for a while. Then I decided that I wanted to go... I went down to a little place called Wewoka. That's right down the road about nineteen miles from Seminole. So I went down there, and I ran into a guy named J.R. Watts, who was a piano player.
What's the name of this town?

Wewoka. It's nineteen miles east of Seminole. And I went down there, and I run into a guy named, like I said, J.R. Watts, the pianist. He had a little rhythm section, just a guitar and him and a drummer. And I told him, I said, I'd run into (what's his name?) A.J. Lottie, who was a trumpet player that I had met when I went there, and a guy named Chan that played trombone. So I told him about it, and I said, well, the three of us could get

together and we could have a little band, you know. So he says, "Okay, you get the guys together." And I said, "Yeah, all right" -- because I was learning how to write, too. So I learned how to write....
You were all self-taught.
Yeah.
And what you picked up from...

And what I picked up from other musicians, yeah. So I wrote out some things for the three horns, and we rehearsed with J.R. until he got us... He finally got a gig for us in Ada, Oklahoma. We went to Ada to play for dancing, that dime a dance thing, you know...
Now, what year was this?

This was... Oh, man, years! I have to stop and think about that. Let's see, what year was it? It was in '34 or '35, somewhere along there. And we went to Ada and played for this dime a dance thing, which was horrible, but I mean, at least it was some money. We were making enough money to eat and so forth.
And I used to go hang out with a cat named Bud Bennett; he played piano on the radio. So I'd go and play with him just so that I could get people to get to know who I was...
You played with him on the radio program?
Yeah, I worked on the radio with him.
When was he on? In the afternoon?

Yeah, in the afternoon. And he would sing. Like, he was jive, a jive piano player, but he could sing, and people liked him and they would listen to him. So when I came on the air, I got a lot of friends through him, you know, in Ada. They had a broadcasting station there, and he used to go out every day, and I'd go out with him, you know, just for something to do, because we didn't have to work until that night with the dime-a-dance thing.
I stayed there for a while. And then J.R. went back to Wewoka. We went right to Wewoka then. He got a gig going out to... He went to a town in New Mexico...Albuquerque.
You went to Albuquerque.

We went to Albuquerque to play. I had met these two guys there, Henry Gray and Hunter Gray, and Jay McShann. But I knew Jay from Muskogee, but I hadn't known the two Gray brothers. So they were out there with a band called...
What did they play?

One played trumpet and one played tenor. So they were out there playing with Jay McShann, and they went to Albuquerque. They were working at a place called Silver's Resort. And the guy that owned the thing was a state commissioner.
Silver's Resort?

Yeah, Silver's Resort. J.R. got the gig out there to replace them. So when I got out there, I saw these guys, and I knew these guys could play, you know, because I had heard them play in Shawnee, Oklahoma one night in a dance, and I'd heard the Gray Brothers, and I know that Jay can play -- so I wanted to be with him. So I told him. He said, 'Well, we got another job we're going on to, so why don't you come on and go with us.'
In the meantime, Watts had me and a guitar and a drum and himself, and I said, 'Well, I can't learn anything just the way they're playing, because I was teaching them' -- because I'm there. It's better I go where I can learn something, and I want to know... I asked Jay would he teach me how to write for the group, so he said 'Yeah.' So we had two trumpets and a tenor and a bass and drums and a singer; he had Bill Powell. So I learned a whole lot from Jay, like all the tunes Earl Hines was playing -- 'Deep Forest' and what was that, 'Bubbling Over'... I don't know whether you know anything about them tunes.
'Deep Forest' I remember.
Yeah, that was his theme song, 'Deep Forest.'
Yeah, right. 'Bubbling Over'?
Yeah. [SINGS 16 BARS] But I wrote that out for the band...
You used to hear these bands on the radio, I guess. You could hear...
Yeah, we could hear Earl Hines and so forth on the radio.
Were you buying records then, too? Did you have records?
No, I didn't have no records.
You didn't have records.
No. We didn't have nothin' to play it on in the first place.
So what kind of a model would you use when you started to do your writing, when you first started to write?

Whatever I heard, I could write. I just had to... Like, Jay taught me the changes on the piano. So I would figure that out, and then I'd write out the instruments for trumpet and tenor. They're all in the same key, so it was easy for me to write them. So I wrote out the trumpet parts and the tenor parts for Henry. It was real easy to do. But without Jay McShann, I don't know what would have happened, because he taught me the changes to most of the tunes that I was trying to write. And I learned all of them, like the tune "I Wished On The Moon" and a
couple more tunes that I remember, if I can think of the name of them -- but that's kind of hard to do, to think of them now.
Had you heard other bands like the Blue Devils by then?

Oh yeah, I heard the Blue Devils in Oklahoma City. They came down there and played a dance, and they sounded pretty nice. But I really didn't know that much about music, so I couldn't say that they were good or that they were...
But you remember hearing them when you were in Oklahoma City.
Oh yeah, yeah. Then my brother, Ben, came through there...
Ben Johnson.
Yeah, with T. Holder. I had heard about him, but I never heard him play -- but I didn't think so much of him, come to think of it.
When was this? Was this in Albuquerque?
No, this is in Oklahoma City.
Oh, back in Oklahoma City.
But getting back to Albuquerque, I met a guy... Also, we had a tenor player, another saxophone player named Lester Taylor. He said he could get me a gig with Gene Coy's band, so...
The Black Aces.

Yeah. So I said... Boy, I got to tell you about that. We played a dance... After I got with the band, we were playing a dance out in Lubbock, Texas. And so some White guy walks up to the band, and it said, "Gene Coy and His Black Aces." He looked up at it, and we had some dark fellows in the band, so the guy says, "Yup, they're plenty dark all right" -- they're plenty Black all right; that's what he really meant. So anyway, I mean, I laughed; I shouldn't have laughed, I guess. And all the guys turned around and looked at me. I said, "Well, I can't help it if you're Black. If you're black, you're Black." But anyway, that was... Oh, I cracked up behind that shit, because I really didn't expect nobody to say nothin' like that, and this cat just come up and looked at 'em, and said, "Yup, you're plenty Black all right." Oh boy, I thought that was funny, but the guys didn't think it was funny. So I learned a lesson from that, never to do that no more, don't laugh about being Black.

So anyway, I was with Gene Coy, and he was coming back through Albuquerque. But Gene Coy didn't pay nobody, you know what I mean? Like, we'd go play and play and play and play and play, and man, he'd wind up probably giving you two dollars or something. I said, "Gee, man, this ain't it."
You could do better on your own.

I was doing better out there in Albuquerque than I was being with this band. So Lester didn't join the band. He went on to Kansas, to Wichita, Kansas, and he told him about me, and he sent for me, and I joined the band like a dummy. I didn't know that I was supposed to get a salary. He didn't give me nothin' me, man. He gave me two dollars maybe every now and then. And then I had to buy my own food and everything, and it was just... It was horrible. I mean, what kind of job is this, where you work and you don't get paid? But anyway, he said he was going to Albuquerque, so I figured I'd wait til I get to Albuquerque and go back with the band that I was with before -- which I did.
But after I went back with the band, they broke up. So the two Gray boys, Hunter and Henry, went to Denver. They knew the guy, Art Bronson, that had a band called the Bostonians....
I've heard of that band I guess because Lester Young played with them.

Yeah, he played with them. Right. So anyway, I told Henry, 'Well, you all get up there and sound that cat and see if he needs another trumpet player. If he does, I'd like to join him, because I ain't got no job.' You know, I'm way out here in Albuquerque and I don't know

too many people. I was supposed to have some kind of cousin out there or something, but I never did find him. But anyway, they went to Denver, and about a week later I got a ticket to come on up to Denver.

And that's when I went up to join Art Bronson and His Bostonians. I don't think nobody in there had ever been to Boston!, ha-ha, now that I think about it, you know. But they was a nice group, you know. Prez wasn't there. I wish he had've been; I'd love to have been there when he was there!
But anyway, I stayed with them for a while, and then Harriet Calloway came through Denver. Have you ever heard of her?
You told me about her when I did that interview for the book that I'm doing.
Oh yeah.
I remember I said, 'Well, I've heard of Blanche Calloway, but I've never heard of Harriet Calloway.' So tell that story.

Well, Harriet Calloway was...she claimed to be Cab's sister, but she really wasn't -- because I found that out from the manager of the band. He liked her and he was booking her. The trumpet player, I think I told you about him.
Well, let's do it again.

Anyway, so I joined the band, and we went up to Cheyenne, we had a bus wreck up in Montana. Basically that group I was with in Albuquerque had also joined the band with me when I joined Harriet's band. So we went up to Winnipeg and down to Grand Rapids, Michigan. And when we got to Grand Rapids, Michigan, Harriet cut out and left the band stranded, you know, without paying the band. Of course, I think that they thought they were slick.

Well, anyway, that's when Charles damn near went haywire, because she couldn't figure out how she could go off and leave him, as tight as he had been with him.
Now, that was the trumpet player, what was his name, Charlie Jacobs?
Charlie Jacobs, right. He was a helluva trumpet player, too, man. I used to marvel at this cat every night. Every time he played he was somethin' else.
You told me he was quite advanced...
Oh, he was.
....for the time.
For the time, he was somethin' else, man. I tell you, he was a bad motherfucker, that's all I can tell you -- because he was bad.
What kind of style did he play in, would you say, if
you could liken it to any style that we know? Was it a little like Roy Eldridge?

Well, he was just as modern as Roy was in them days. But he didn't play like Roy. He had a nice sound, though. He had a nice tone. And he could play. I used to marvel at him. I used to say, 'I wish I could play like that.'
And he was going with Harriet Calloway...
Yeah.
And when she cut out, he...

Yeah, he flipped. He didn't know what to do. But he followed her all the way to Seattle, you know; and they had quite a problem out there, I hear. But anyway, they didn't get back together. So I don't know what happened to him. I never heard of him any more. But he was a helluva trumpet player, though, man. I brag about him now. I was telling Dizzy about him. Charlie Jacobs was somethin' else. He had such a beautiful sound, man. You know, when he played, you couldn't help but listen.

So now, getting back to where I was at...
Out in Grand Rapids.
In Grand Rapids.
What year are we in now?
Oh, this would have to be around '36 or '37,

somewhere along there. Anyway, a guy named Terry, who played piano, came to Grand Rapids to get some musicians. He heard the band was stranded there, and he came to pick up some musicians, because he had a job working at some restaurant in Minot, North Dakota. And he hired me and the bass player...
[PAUSE]
So now we're in Grand Rapids. This guy Terry, the piano player, came...
Yeah, he came and got us.
For Minot, North Dakota.

Yeah, for Minot. So anyway, we went to Minor, and we worked there for a while. And there was another band there named Herb Whitfield. He had a group working at a hotel. After this gig that Terry had folded, he sounded me and the bass player to come work with him, which we did. You know, naturally, you've got to keep working, and when you're poor you can't say no to no job. So we went on down there, and we started to work there. And I learned how to write for the... I knew the trumpet and tenor, I'd been writing music, so I started writing for that band. And everybody liked the tunes that I was writing, so I kept it up.
What kind of things were you writing then?

Swing things mostly, you know. I mean, I was listening to Roy, too; I could hear him from Chicago. And I had kind of changed a little bit from Louis to Roy, because I liked Roy and I liked what he was playing -- because he was really playing in them days.

I'd never heard nobody else play like that except Charlie Jacobs. And Charlie, I couldn't hear him. He was out somewhere... Where he went, I don't know. But anyway, he went haywire, because after he found out that Harriet was gone he just went completely... He couldn't believe it, man. I said, "Well, she's gone. Just believe that, will you? You don't have to believe whether she loves you or not. Just believe that she ain't here no more. She's gone on out." But I'll tell you, when a man's in love, you can't talk to him. He don't hear nothin'.
And like I was saying, I was listening to Roy.

Shortly after that, his gig run out, we stayed at a hotel until this gig ran out, then we went from there to Bismarck and played someplace over there. It was cold... Oh boy, it was colder than the world's biggest fanny, boy, I'll tell you.
When that job run out... There was a piano player there in Bismarck, so she sounded me and the bass player and the drummer if we'd go to Fargo with her, because she had a job

in Fargo. And I had to work, and I said, "Well, shit, yeah, the hell with Herb Whitfield. If he ain't got no job, I won't stay here with him. Let him get a job, and then he can come talk to me." So we went to Fargo. And they liked the group, but they didn't like the piano player -- and it was her gig, you know. So they fired her, and then they come back and hire each one individually. Which was all right, because at least we kept the money coming in. And me and the bass player... I had to double on trumpet and piano, one hand with the piano and one on trumpet, you know. You can imagine how that sounded then; I was a horrible trumpet player at that stage anyway, you know. I didn't know what I was doing.
Well, you couldn't have been horrible. You'd been playing with all these bands. You must have had some kind of...
Yeah, but I wasn't talkin' about nothin'. I mean, I had heard Roy, and I know that I wasn't talkin' about nothin', you know. So I said, "Well, shit, I've got to make a living," so...
One hand on the piano and one hand on the trumpet.
One hand on the piano and the other on the trumpet. That's the way I had to do that.
The last guy I saw do that was Charlie Moffett, the
drummer who used to play with Ornette Coleman. He played the drums with one hand and the trumpet with the other!
He did?
Yeah!
I don't think I heard him.
That was a long time ago, before he had his family... Anyway, to get back to... So here you were up in Fargo, doing this.
Yeah. So pretty soon that job run out. And we said, "Where should we go from here, Bassy and I?" I said, "Well, let's go to Minneapolis.
You mean the bass player?
Yeah. I said, "Let's go to Minneapolis." So we had enough bus fare to get...
Were these all like the first time you had been to any of these places?
Yeah, first time, you know. So I didn't really know what to do in Minneapolis. I guess God was looking out for me...
But I guess that was the biggest city you had been to.

Yeah, it was the biggest city that I had been to besides Denver and Albuquerque, and they wasn't no big cities really. So I went to Minneapolis. And just by chance, it was on a Sunday, and I went into this after-hours

joint -- they had after-hours joints I'd play. And that's where I met Oscar Pettiford and the Pettiford Family, the brothers and... Let me see, who else did I meet up there? That bass player, a helluva bass player. Adolphus...
Adolphus Alsbrook.
Yeah, I met him...
I can never get whether it's Alsbrook or Allbrook...
Alsbrook.
Milt Hinton has talked about him quite a bit.

Yeah, I met him out there. And luckily, I met a piano player up there who was looking for a trumpet player, so he asked me was I working, and I said, "You got a job?" He said, "Yeah." I said, "Well, I am now. Well, what it is." So he was working in St. Paul. Anyway, I went over to St. Paul to work for him, and thank goodness, because it was colder than a son-of-a-bitch. You talk about cold, boy, St. Paul and Minneapolis was out of sight.

Minot was cold, too. I got double pneumonia up there. It was really cold. Me and Bassy were staying together. He was a big guy, and every time he'd turn over, all the blankets and shit would go with him.
What was his name?
Homer Woods.
Homer Woods?
Yeah. He was a helluva bass player, though. He played a big tuba and shit, you know. I learned a lot from him, because I listened to him play.
I guess a lot of the bass players or tuba players did both in those days.
Oh yeah. Well, they didn't have no bass. They just had a bass horn, you know. Because I never seen a bass fiddle with any band.
Until when?
Until I got with... I guess it was much later, after I left Minneapolis and...
Well, what was Pettiford playing and Alsbrook?
Well, they were playing it, but I wasn't working with them, so I really didn't know nothin' about the bass.
So in other words, every band you worked with up until then was all tuba?
All tuba, yeah.
So when you call him the bass, you mean he was playing the bass parts.

Yeah. So I learned what he was doing with the bass, which helped me, too. At least it helped me in the music end of it; not that it really did anything for me. And back when I was working over in St. Paul, I met...

Who was this guy? He played trumpet. My memory fails me here. This guy had a little group that worked right up the street from us. I thought I would learn something by working with him, so I went with him, but I shouldn't have. I should have stayed where I was at in the first place. I was happy there and didn't realize it. L. Herbert, that's what his name was.
L. Herbert?
Yeah. He had a band in St. Paul. I was working with a cat named Joe Cephus, and I left him to go with this Al Herbert, but really he wanted me to play tenor, and shit, I wasn't no tenor player.
Had you played any reeds since you put the clarinet down?

No, I hadn't played any, but I knew how to play the tenor and I knew how to... You know, I had tried to play it, but man, like, my chops wasn't ready for the reeds. I'm used to playing on a trumpet. And it kind of held me up, you know.
He didn't want any two-trumpet group, in other words.

No, he didn't want me to play trumpet. I could out-play him playing trumpet, so he said, 'You play the saxophone.' But he had a helluva saxophone player, Harry Pettiford -- he was a helluva tenor man, you know.

And I took his place. So nobody's walking in behind that man, because that man can really play the tenor saxophone. Me, I was just learning the damn thing, hardly just about learning it. And I didn't do so good.

So I had to cut out from that band. I went with a trio down to Rochester, Minnesota, where the Mayo Clinic is. We went down there, and that's when they brought in Social Security... I guess I went around '36 or '37, or '38 maybe. The guy started collecting Social Security. So we didn't understand what the fuck they meant. In fact, I didn't know what Social Security meant. In fact, for me it was just like somebody was taking my money, you know. So we had to go through with it, because we had to finish the job, and so we stayed until the job was over. And that's where I got my first Social Security card.

Then the next thing I know, we was back in St. Paul, and I had to join the union, because I had a pretty nice little job playing up there -- I can't think of the name of the club to save my soul. Some joint out there. Aw, what the heck is it? I've been trying to think of the name of that club, and I can't think of it.
It will come to you.
I hope so. It ain't come to me in years, man. I've been trying to figure out what's the name of this
club.
The only one I ever heard of, I think, was later, but I don't know how it was going...was the Nest. There was a place called the Nest that they talk about.
No, man.
It wasn't that.

No, it wasn't that. It was some joint up there. Anyway, I had to join the union. I (?) with that, because I couldn't see what I was joining the union for. I'd been working all the time anyway, you know.

So anyway, I got a letter from this guy named Bernie Young in Milwaukee. I had met this saxophone player, and he had told me about Bernie Young, and I sounded him, you know, if he could get me a job, I'd come and join the band. So he said for me to come on and join the band. That was another mistake! Because they were on the WPA, do you know what that is?
Works Project Administration.

Yeah. See, all of the band was on that. So when I joined it, I went there, they didn't give a shit about working. You know, they was workin' anyway! So I'm there, and I ain't got no money and I ain't got no job... I mean, I got a job but they don't work!
They just get paid.

They just get paid, you know. I said, 'Well, what the fuck happens to me?' I'm here and I can't stay with this group, and have nothing happen. So I started writing for a cat named Bailey. He had a sextet.
Bailey?
Yeah. A tenor player.
This is in Milwaukee.
Yeah, in Milwaukee.
It's interesting to see the way you moved from place to place, getting to every state in that area.
Yeah. Wait til you see what happened to me later. I was writing arrangements for this guy...
For Bailey.
Yeah. He didn't pay too much, but I'd just write because I could hear my music played, and I needed the experience anyway. I just kept writing for him until Leonard Gay, I know you heard of him...
Mmm-hmm.

A tenor player from Milwaukee. He decided to put an eight-piece band together and play at the Cotton Club in Milwaukee, which he did. And they had another trumpet player named Leo Shoats, he and I was the brass. And Larry Gay, and he had another tenor player...I can't think of his name. Anyway, John White played alto. It was
a good band... For me I mean, because I could experiment with the horns, you know, and I could really find get to find out what to do with it. So I enjoyed it. I loved it.
Was it five horns or four horns?
Five horns and three rhythm. And Stanley Overton on piano, P.G. on drums. Let me see, who was the bass player? Hank something...I can't think of his name.
Anyway...
Anyway, he didn't make it. He wasn't that great a bass player in the first place. I guess I shouldn't really mention him. But he was there.

And we went from there... From the Cotton Club, we went to the Cotton Club in Cincinnati, and we stayed there for a while -- six months, I think. Then Gay decided he wanted to come back to Milwaukee. Now, what he wanted to come back to Milwaukee for, I don't know, because he didn't have no job there, and I know when I go back to Milwaukee ain't nothin' happenin' but that WPA band, and I ain't gonna be in that motherfucker no more. I said, "That's it."
You mean they never worked, the WPA band?

No, man... They worked... Every now and then they might get a gig, you know. But the money was no good, see, like maybe five or six dollars. And like, what can you do with that after you're gonna pay your rent and live?
So I got a job with a guy named Tommy Fox up there...
In Milwaukee.
In Milwaukee. But this was to go up in Duluth... This was Superior.
Yeah, Duluth and Superior up there on the lake.
Yeah. Talkin' about cold, boy oh boy... I thought Minot was bad, but man, Duluth and Superior were somethin' else.
[PAUSE]

And I stayed up there for six months, bought me a new Martin trumpet. I thought I was doing something, plus I was making thirty-five dollars a week, every week, which was a godsend. I needed it, boy, because it sure was cold up there. I swear, man! Whew. So I'll never forget that.

And Tommy Fox, the bandleader, he lost his son up there on the lake, Lake Superior. He and his son and his daughter went out swimming. Anyway, the boy got drowned, because he didn't know how to swim that good. Which was a sad affair, because it was a band affair. Tommy was a beautiful cat, and we all loved him and everything, but we couldn't help it about his son, because he was a beautiful son.
But anyway, when we came back down to Milwaukee, I got a notice from a cat named Step Wharton. Do you know him?
Step Wharton. I've heard of the name.
A piano player.
Yeah.
Anyway, he had a band, a big band. And he needed a trumpet player.
What year is this? Where are we? Are we still in '38?

Yeah, or '39. No, wait a minute. We went to Cincinnati to the Cotton Club, right? Then we went back up to Superior, Wisconsin for six months, and then we came back and then I joined Step. So that would make it about '39 or '40, the early part of '40 maybe. Yeah, I think it was the early part of '40, because shortly after that I went with Jimmy Rochelle in Michigan.
So you kept working your way over.
Well, I had to. That's one thing, you know, if you want to improve yourself, you've got to keep moving wherever you can move. So that's what I did.
[PAUSE]
You were with Step Wharton.
I'm with Step Wharton now. This is after...
After Superior, yeah.
Okay. So Step Wharton's band broke up, because there were no gigs. So I went with Jimmy Rochelle, and they had...
This was in Michigan?
Yeah.
Did you go to Michigan?
Yeah. Well, they sent for me.
Where was he? In Detroit?
No, he wasn't in Detroit.
Not yet.
In Battle Creek and Kalamazoo and places like that.
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE 1]
Let's see, Jimmy Rochelle. Yeah, we played a lot of places, like in Battle Creek, Lansing, Kalamazoo, Grand Forks.
What kind of a band did he have?
It was pretty good. He had Milt Buckner and Wardell Gray, myself, and a cat named Duck who played trumpet...
Would you say this was the best band you had played with up to that point?
Yeah, I think it was about the best band. No, Step Wharton's band was the best band, but Jimmy's band wasn't bad, because with Milt Buckner and Wardell...
You had some good soloists.

We had some good soloists, yeah. The type of music he was playing wasn't so hot, but he had good musicians in the band. Because I used to write... Buckner used to write for the band and I'd write for the band. So we did all right as far as the music was concerned, except that he was really one of those bands that played for dancing and so forth and so on, and that's the type of jobs he had. They wasn't really nothin' outlandishly what you really dug.
Like, Leonard Gay I think was the best Swing band that I had played with up until then.
But Jimmy Rochelle had a good band. I mean, he kept working all the time, and he paid a fair wage. It wasn't nothin' to brag about, but it wasn't nothin' to cry about either.

So I stayed with him until I got a job in Detroit working with a six-piece band. I think his name was Hayes, a tenor player -- Tubby, they called him. Not Tubby Hayes. This is Tubby we called him. And he had a guy named Johnny something who played piano, and Freddie Radcliff played the drums...
Freddie Radcliff. I remember him.
Yeah, he was in the band. Charles Johnson played alto saxophone. He was in the band. And I don't

know whether you heard of him, but he ended up in Buffalo. I think he went to Buffalo after he left...after the band broke up, you know. We stayed together for quite a while. We worked out in River Rouge.
River Rouge where the famous Ford plant...
Yeah. Well, we used to play out there every weekend, you know.
I guess Detroit and that whole area was always such a...
It was much better than most towns. At least they had work...
There were people working and they had money to spend.

That's right. But when I was there... When they first took me to Detroit, it wasn't shit happening there. I think that was back in 1927 or '29 or somewhere back there. My old man, he got laid off and he had to split.
That's why he went back to Oklahoma.

Yeah. Well, he had sense enough to do that. Because in Oklahoma he was all right, he did all right. He got ahold of some money and had a store, and put his brother in business, and told him that this was supposed to be mine -- which I never got. But I didn't...
You weren't supposed to do that anyway.
No, I wasn't supposed to have it no way. But anyway, that's some of the things that happen to you.
Anyway, here you are in Detroit working with this six-piece band.
Yeah.
Is this 1940?
Yeah, this is 1940. And I stayed with the band until I think almost up until '41.
When did you take your own band into the Club Congo?
This is what I'm coming to right now. I went into the Club Congo. It was a good band, too. But I came through there, and Hamp changed my mind about the whole situation.
How did he do that?
Well, he offered me a job! Ha-ha. I figured... I said, what I'm gonna do is either stay here and work in this joint... And it was really a good job. I mean...
Well, you had a 12-piece band, I understand.
A 12-piece band. Yeah, it was nice.
And you wrote for the band?
Yeah.
And you had the show?
Yeah, we played for the shows.
And played for dancing and the whole thing?
Yeah. But Hamp persuaded me to give that up and come with him.
But what kind of place was the Club Congo?
It was just a joint where people go and drink and dance and so forth, and they put on the show twice a night.
Like with a shake dancer and a comedian and the whole thing?
Yeah. Mills Brothers and all them...
Oh, you had some headliners.

All the headliners came in, yeah. Well, I made a fortune out of the club, because most of the acts that came in, they didn't have no music, and they had to have music. So I would write for... You know, I would tell them, 'Well, I'll write the music for you' and charge them so much for it, you know. So I made a fortune... Like, I did very good in that club.
How long were you at the Congo, would you say?
About six months. Maybe a little longer than that, I don't know. But anyway...
Who was in the band? Anybody that we would know?
Well, let's see. I don't know whether you would know these people or not. Let's see. Johnny Young
played piano...
Not the one that's in Chicago.
Oh, no...
A different John Young.
This is a different John Young. Let's see. Well, I don't think you'd know any of these guys. Most of them was from Detroit. You know Kelly Martin.
Yeah. He was the drummer.
Yeah, he was the drummer. And we had... I'm trying to think it was we had on tenor. Wardell came in after I left, but they had another tenor player there. Okay... Where did I go from there...?
Well, then Hamp came through town and heard you...
Yeah. Well, then Hamp talked to me about come and join him.
He had heard you at the Congo?
Yeah. That's where he heard me. He said, 'Yeah, Gates, you gotta come with me.' I said, 'All right,' 'so... Me like a dummy, I was saying, 'Yeah, I guess I will.' I figured here's a big-name...
Right. This is your first really big name.
Right. Big name going...
National.
Yeah. I'll probably get into something,

you know. Well, you never know. I'll tell you, when Gladys paid me off, she said, "What is this here?" She handed me two ten dollar bills. We played two nights and she handed me twenty dollars. I said, "What is this?" She said, "Well, this is your salary." I said, "Salary? I was making seventy dollars a week in Detroit, and I quit that to come out here. I can't go for this kind of money." So she said, "Well, you either have to go back or forget it, because we don't pay no more than that." And I was so amazed, because I didn't know that they...
Didn't you discuss salary in front?
No! I just took it for granted that...
That they paid well.
Yeah, that they paid well. It was a big-name band. I figured what the hell.
Who was with the band then?
Everybody that Hamp brought to New York with him. Joe Newman, Ernie Royal, Marshall Royal, Illinois Jacquet, Dexter Gordon -- that same band.
It was a hot band.
Yeah. And they ain't payin' no money! Ten dollars a night. I said, "No good, baby." I say, "I'll go back to Detroit first." So I quit the band and went back to Detroit, and just...
How long were you with Hamp?
About two weeks. You ain't gonna work for a man that ain't gonna pay you. I said, "Shit, I don't need this. I'll go back to Detroit."
Had you seen Ernie and Marshall like since Oklahoma, between...?
No, I hadn't seen them. Well, I didn't know that they played...
But did you all remember each other?

Yeah, I remembered Ernie. I didn't remember Marshall too well [LAUGHS], but I remembered Ernie. Because Ernie was a helluva trumpet player. When I heard him he was doing that shit in B-flat, jumpin' out. I said, "Goddamn, he really learned something since I seen him." I don't know how he learned it, but he did. Anyway...
So you never went to New York with the band.

No, no. I quit the band. After we played the Regal Theatre in Chicago I said, "That's it. I'm going back to Detroit. I ain't goin' nowhere with this band." Man, not with ten dollars a night. I was making more than that in Detroit, and I didn't have to go...
Without going out on the road.
Yeah, without being out on the road. So I went back to Detroit, and as soon as I got there I got a
telegram from Andy Kirk, telling me to join him...
Well, how did he know about you?
I think the manager from Hamp's band had told him that I was a good trumpet player. Because I know nobody else wouldn't have known about me out East.
Where was Kirk at the time?
He was in New York. That's where I got the wire from. So he told me to meet...
This must be '41, right?

Yeah. He told me to meet the band in St. Louis. And I said, "Oh yeah? Okay" -- at the Tune Town Ballroom. So I went on out there and met him. He was a beautiful cat when I first... The first time I met him, he was really beautiful. He said, "Well, how are you?" I said, "Oh, I'm fine, sir. I'm fine. Yeah, how you doin'?" So he talked to me. He said, "Well, I don't have no uniforms, so you'll just have to wear a tuxedo." And I said, "Well, that's all right. I've got one." But then again, I said, "How much do I get?" So he said, "The best I can do right now is seventeen dollars a night." I said, "Okay, that's all right. I can go for that." So I told Billy Shaw two weeks later, I said, "I asked Andy for a raise, and he told me to see you, said it's all right with him." So he did. He raised me up to nineteen dollars. I
said, "Now, this sounds more like what I was interested in." And the longer I stayed there, every time I'd go to Billy for a raise, I would get it!
Billy Shaw was the manager?
Billy Shaw. He was our manager, yeah.
I think you told me you were writing for that band, too.
Yeah, yeah.
You weren't with Hamp long enough to write for him.

No, I had my own music playing with Hamp, so when I got ready to leave, I just took it up. I just sort of passed it in. Every time we'd play a number that I wrote, I would pass that in. So I took my music with me and I put it in Kirk's band, and it sounded good like a motherfucker. We swung the shit out of it.
Who was in Kirk's band at that time?
Oh, they had Harold Baker, Big Jim Lawson and myself, and Bill Coleman...
Bill Coleman?
Yeah.
That's a good trumpet section.
Yeah, it was good. And Al Sears, Ben Smith, Harrington and John Williams.
Was that the alto player?
Harrington was their alto player.
Yeah, but John Williams played alto and baritone?
He played baritone.
That wasn't the same one that married Mary Lou Williams.
Yeah, that was the same one. But she was going with Harold Baker at that time.
Uh-huh. Now, was she in the band?
Yeah, she was in the band. Her and Booker Collins.
Booker Collins. And Ben Thigpen?
Yeah, and Thigpen. That's the first time I'd ever worked with any name band.
So that was the first time you met Mary Lou.
Yeah.
She must have been quite impressive.

Oh, she was. I went to her and asked her what do you use for chords, like, to play when you play "Indiana," and she showed me like where you put in the substitute chords like A-flat, G-flat, F-7 to B-flat, instead of going [DE-DA-DA-DA] and then go to F-7, DE-DA-DA-DA, and then go to B-flat-7, and each change you add that F-sharp in there...
Was she the first one that...
That hipped me to that.
That showed you those kind of things.
Those kinds of things, yeah. You know, I didn't know you could do that even with music. I found out you could.

So I really enjoyed being with Kirk, because he let me play anything I wanted to play. He never said, "Well, I want you to do this, I want you to do that." He said, "Okay, if that's what you want, we'll do it." Which was beautiful. And we came to New York, and they made me play "McGhee Special" ten times before they decided to record it. So I was just on the verge of giving him some, "Fuck it, I don't want to make it, the hell with it," blah-blah-blah, and then the guy said, "Okay, let's make it now."
When had you written that?
Oh, I wrote that back there when I was in the band in Detroit.
Where? At the Congo?
Yeah.
When you had your own band.
Yeah.
You wrote that for the...
Yeah, for me.
A feature.
My feature.
A feature for yourself.
Yeah.
Was it always called "McGhee Special"?
Yeah.
That's what you called it.

Yeah, that's what I called it, right. But I did that... I just took the book and I put the arrangement in Andy's band, and Andy featured me on it. You know, after hearing it, he liked it, and he said, "Well, it looks good; we'll keep it in the book." And most of my music he liked, you know. I wrote "Seven Come Eleven" and things that Benny made...
"Seven Come Eleven"?

Yeah, I wrote that up for him. And quite a few things I wrote. And all of June Richmond's vocals I was doing. With Andy I was having a ball, man. The money was nice, and every time I asked for a raise I'd get one. So I got it up to thirty-five dollars a night...
And the band was a pretty happy band, I guess, with each other...
With each other. We were getting along beautiful. In fact, I hated to leave the band, but I really left the band on account of money.
What happened?
Well, I went with Charlie Barnet, see. And that made a difference, because Charlie...
Was that in '43?

In '42, I think. Yeah, I think it was at that time. But then, I really traveled after that...with Barnet, I mean. I went back with Kirk, because Charlie said he was going to take off six months -- he didn't want to play no more for a while. And after he was off a month, he called me up... I was with Andy, and he called me up telling me he got a contract on me; and I didn't remember signing no contract with him.
Well, how long had you been with Barnet when he decided to lay off for a while?
About a year.
A year.
Yeah.
I remember you telling me that you'd asked him for a raise, and he would cry poverty, and yet he'd be out gambling...
He'd be out gambling, yeah...
And losing all his money.
And losing all his money. Yeah, I was telling you about when he was in Atlantic City. He was
gambling and shooting dice.
In Atlantic City it was?

Yeah. He was shooting dice. It wasn't like it is now! But man, this cat, he would throw away more money in one night than I had made in a whole damn year. Then I asked him for a raise and he wouldn't give me a raise. I said, "Oh boy, this cat is something. It's hard to believe a motherfucker could be like this." And he'd take me out with him and let me see him doing it. Then when I asked him for some money, he said "No!" Man...
Before we get to this bit about the contract, tell me a little bit about the Barnet band and playing on it.
Who was in it and all that?
Yeah. Well, you weren't the first Black guy to play on the band?
No, no, Peanuts Holland was the first, I guess. I guess, I don't know. Maybe he had somebody Black before that. I don't know..
I don't know. But then, of course, he had Trummy...
Yeah, but that was afterwards.
And he had Dizzy for a little bit.
Afterwards.
And Oscar. Oscar was on it with you.
Yeah. I got Oscar the gig.
Right. You told me that story, in Minneapolis...
Yeah.
Now, had you seen Oscar and the other Pettifords after that one time in Minneapolis?
No.
Not until you came through with Barnet.
Well, we used to hang out when I lived in Minneapolis, you know.
Yeah.
But when we was going to Minneapolis I told Charlie... I said, "Charlie, I've got a bass player I want you to hear."
Had you been back to Minneapolis?
No, I hadn't been back to Minneapolis.
So you went with Charlie.
Yeah, I went with Charlie. And I told Pettiford to come down to the theatre, and he came down and played, and Charlie hired him right away -- boom, yeah, you're hired.
And that got Chubby uptight.
Yeah. Chubby didn't like that shit. I can understand that...
We're talking about Chubby Jackson, of course.
Well, I can understand Chubby being mad,
because Oscar was cookin'. He was bad.
Oscar is probably one of the handful of the greatest bassists who ever played.
Yeah, because when I first heard him, I didn't believe him either. Man, this cat is out of sight. He was something else. Now, we...
Well, we're still talking about Barnet.

We're still about Barnet, yeah. Well, Barnet hired him immediately, and Chubby got nervous. Chubby's fingers were like that, right. He was shakin' and everything. I can understand that, because Pettiford... If a trumpet player had walked in and sounded as good as Pettiford sounded over Chubby and sounded that good over me, I'd be shaking like that, too, man.
But then eventually they did a routine together.
Yeah, a dance number...
Wasn't it "Salt and Pepper" or something?
Yeah. They did a dance routine together.
And they used to play some two-bass things?
Yeah. Well, they had to get along. If they were working together, they had to get along. And that was beautiful.
How as it, though, to be a Black man in a White band like that?
Well, it was all right, except that...
I guess there were really no problems with the people i the band.
No, wasn't no problems with the people in the band. Charlie wouldn't go for that shit. If you was prejudiced, you didn't have no business being there, and he let you know that right away.

But there were a few occasions where an incident come up... Like, the road manager wouldn't put my name down on the thing for a reservation for a room or something in White hotels in the... We went to Worcester. Now, you know Worcester is not a real prejudiced place. But he didn't put the names down. So when I went to go check in, I heard someone say, "Well, give him a key for Howard McGhee." And he says, "No, no-no, we don't have no Howard McGhee on here." So I was the only one in the band... No, Peanuts was there, too.
This is before Pettiford.
Yes, this is before Pettiford.
So you and Peanuts were...

Yeah, we were there. So the guy said, "We don't have no more rooms anyway." So I said, "Oh well..." The next day at rehearsal... Charlie had called a rehearsal for ten o'clock that morning. So the next morning I didn't

show up for rehearsal. So he was mad... Charlie was madder than a wet hen. When I came in the theatre, he said, "Where you been?!" I said, "I was trying to find a place to stay? Why? Did you have a place for me to stay?" So he said, "Oh... What's the matter? Why didn't you stay at the hotel like everybody else?" I said, "Well, I didn't have no reservation there." So... I think Mort was the road manager then. So he said...
Mort who?

I can't think of his last name. Morty, yeah, that's right. Anyway, Charlie said, "Get him. Tell him I said come here." So I said, "You tell him. I ain't gonna tell him nothin'." I said, "He don't like me; at least he didn't get no room." I said, "I had to walk all night damn near before I found a place to sleep." So when I went to sleep I wasn't thinking about getting up to make no ten o'clock rehearsal."

So he fired him right on the spot. He said, "How come you didn't have the rooms reserved for Holland and McGhee." He said, "You didn't tell me to make them reservations." So Charlie said, "Well, they're in the band, ain't they, fool?" Oh boy, it was something else, man.
But you know, you'd run into some instances like that. A couple of times you'd run into some situations where...
He didn't go South, did he?
Charlie?
Yeah.
No, he wouldn't go South. He wouldn't go South. I had an incident there with Georgie Auld about that shit, though...
Well, we'll get to that later. But I guess Charlie was one of the White bands that played the Apollo, because I remember hearing him there.
Yeah, we played the Apollo several times. In fact, we played everywhere, except anywhere below the Mason-Dixon Line. We'd never go down there.

He said, "No, I'm fine, man." He said, "Get me my clothes; I'm ready to go." I said, "Well, it ain't quite like that, Bird. I can't get you out like that. You have to go to court and all that shit. I don't know what the fuck they got against you, but they got something against you." And I said, "It sounds kind of bad." He said, "What is it?" I said, "I think they got you for nudity." In California they don't like for you to do nothin' wrong. They'll throw the book for the least little thing you do. "So you have to go to court for that."

So he went to court, and they put him in Camarillo to see if he's crazy or insane, because they really don't understand nobody here sittin' on top of a car buck naked. They don't dig that! And that's what they did to Bird. They put him in the thing there. And I used to go there all the time, and I'd take Doris out there to see him and keep track of him, to see if he was all right. And Bird...

Bird was all right. He ran the psychiatrists crazy. There was a cat that was supposed to be taking care of him...? -- and Bird was taking care of him! He was talking about things, and this cat didn't know what Bird was talking about. Bird would talking some heavy shit! Because Bird knew what was going on. Let's face it, he had a mind that was somethin' else. He could talk to you about anything you wanted to talk about.

You could ask him about a carburetor, he'd tell you how to fix it and so forth. Because one night we was driving along, and my car started chug-chug, like it wasn't getting enough gas. So Bird said, "Pull over to the side." So he walked into... We pulled up to a thing with (?), went in there and screwed up something, and he said, "Now start it up, Maggie." So I started it up, and it ran just like brand-new! I said, "Yeah!" I didn't even know what the hell he did. He had adjusted the carburetor so that the air
wasn't getting in there too much, the gas was flowing even...

So Bird was a smart guy. A lot of people didn't know that, but Bird had a mind on him that was something else. Well, his horn tells you that! His music, man, whatever he played, it was right, correct, and you can't see that... There was nothing wrong with it.

A funny thing, too, I was just reminded of it... I asked Johnny Hodges, when Bird first come on the scene... I said to him, "What do you think of Charlie Parker?" He said, "Ah, he don't play nothin'. He don't play nothin'." I said, "No?" He said, "He ain't got no sound." I said, "Charlie Parker ain't got no sound?" So I said, "Okay." So I got a chance... When I worked with Duke, I asked Johnny... It's the first thing I did. I said, "What do you think...?"
How many years later was that?

This was way later. I said, "What do you think of Charlie Parker?" He said, "Oh, he was beautiful." I said, "But Johnny, you told me he didn't have no sound." He said, "Well, I didn't know what I was talking about. He's one of the baddest..." But I mean, that was after they had made that Blues thing...
Right, for Norman Granz.
Yeah. Ha-ha, Bird let everybody know where
he was at. But anyway, I just brought that up because I think that people should know about such things.
Yes, I do, too.
People say...
"Funky Blues."

Yeah. Just a funky blues, and Bird played the shit out of it! Johnny Hodges, I felt sorry for him, because if I was him, I wouldn't have played! "Let him finish making this record; I don't want to make this one." But boy, it was somethin' else.
So you went out to see him quite often...
Oh yeah.
And eventually got his release.

Yeah. Well, what's his name, Ross Russell had a lot to do with that. He went out there... Like I told you, Bird ran this psychiatrist crazy. In fact, he committed suicide, that guy did -- that psychiatrist. He had never met nobody like Bird. He didn't believe nobody could be like him. But Bird had a hell of a mind on him, man. He knew what he was doing and he knew what he was talking about.
I guess that drugs does do something to you, makes you aware of what's happening, going on in the world. Because I didn't know nothin' about all this shit he was talking

about. I didn't know nothin' about it. I hadn't even heard of Stravinsky. Now, you know where I was. I was a dumb stud when it comes to knowing my own music. But Bird hipped me to a lot of things I didn't know about.
But anyway, after we got Bird out of Camarillo, we went into a place called the Hi-De-Ho Club. It was just me and Bird and Hampton Hawes, and Dingbod and Roy Porter.
This was '47?
Yeah, this was in the last part of...
No, it had to be the beginning...
Yeah.
The last part of '46 and the beginning of '47.
Yeah, and the beginning of '47. No, it had to be a little further down than that. I think they kept him in there until '47.
Well, he came back to New York in the Spring, but he made that record date with you...it must have been February or March or something like that.
Yeah, I think it was done in March.
When you did "Carvin' the Bird" and all those things.
Yeah, that was around March.
Then he came back to New York after that.
Well, no... Then we went into this club and we worked together there. Then we played a gig in Chicago
at the Pershing... We played a couple of one-night stands there and in Gary, Indiana. And then we came to New York. I came to New York with him, but I wasn't hangin' out with him.
So when the two of you were in Chicago, it was the two of you with a local...

Yeah, with a local rhythm section. That was in '47. Because we got... He came on back to New York City, and I came to New York, too, but I came and hung out with Fats. Then I had to go back to join Norman in Detroit to play a couple of one-night gigs with him for the Jazz at the Philharmonic.
Now, let's dovetail back a little bit. You had been doing Jazz at the Philharmonics from the time you were in California.
Oh yeah.
What do you remember about that?
What do I remember about it? Well, what is there to remember, except...
Well, how did you meet Norman and what do you remember about...?
Oh, I was with Bean then. The first night we played at Long Beach, that was the first night we hit in California. And Norman Granz came up and heard Bean

playing, so he wanted Bean to make this concert with him. In the meantime, he heard me play and he said would I like to make it also. I said, "yeah, I'd like to make it, but I didn't know what was going on as far as bread was concerned. So I asked Bean about it: "Bean, what do you think I should charge this cat to do this concert?" Bean said, "I don't know. Whatever you want to charge him. Charge him anything." I said, "Well, you're a lot of help. I'm trying to help you; I thought maybe you'd try to help me." He said, "Well, I can't tell you what to charge nobody. You charge him what you want." And that's what happened.
Because you were on that "How High The Moon," which is the one that really put him on the map.
Yeah, it really set him off. Well, frankly, I didn't know my ass from a hole in the ground as far as my business...

Well, we were back with Norman Granz at Jazz at the Philharmonic. So the first one you did was the "How High The Moon" date?
Oh yeah.
Or was there something before that?
No, there was nothing before that.
That was the first one.
That was the first one.
Then you did quite a number of them.
Yeah..
But Charlie Ventura was on that one, and Joe Guy and Willie Smith...
Right.
Then you did one with Dizzy and Bird... But you did several. And you continued to tour for him over the years.
Yes.
But California was... Really, the thing was these jam sessions. Gene Norman started doing them, Just Jazz concerts.
Yeah. Well, Norman really was the one that took the cream. He was the one that had the real inside track. But he was lucky that the "How High The Moon" album sold that many records.
Yeah, that really hit...
Everybody bought that one.
Yeah, really. Because I think that was the first time that kind of live jam session atmosphere was really captured on a record. As soon as you heard it, you wanted it. That got a lot of air play.
Yeah, and most people bought it. That's why I say he got straight behind that one.

I was walking down the street in Los Angeles when I heard me playing. And I said, "What the fuck... I wonder what the hell is this. I know I ain't made no records since I been out here." So I go in the store, and I say, "What is that record you just got through playing?" He said, "Oh, that's the new volume of Jazz at the Philharmonic." I said, "Oh yeah? Who is putting that record out?" Then he told me Asch and Norman Granz. And I said, "Oh yeah?"

So I called Norman, and I said, "Hey, Norman, you put out that record, right?" He said, "Oh yeah, didn't you get your check yet?" I said, "What check?" He said, "Oh, I'll put a check in the mail to you." I said, "You dig?" I said, "Well, now, what is this," you know. So I went to the union, I said, "This man got a record out on me, and I haven't gotten paid for it. He said he's sending me a check." So the guy tells me, he said, "Well, Fain [Elmer Fain] said if he sends you over thirty dollars, that's all we can do." I said, "Yeah? That's all?" He said, "Yeah, that's all we can do." So I said, "Okay, well, if that's what the union says, that's the way it is." So I got a check from Norman; he gave me seventy dollars.
Plus you had gotten paid for the gig

Yeah, that was thirty dollars. So that was a yard I made for the whole thing. So he got straight behind it! And from then on... Well, he considered me a California boy, because that's where I met him, out in California. But I mean, I was really from New York, and I knew more about what was going on than he thought I did.

Anyway, he said, "Look, I want you to make a tour with me." So I said to myself, I know he ain't gonna pay me no money... I knew what he was paying Jacquet and I knew what he was paying the rest of the guys, so I sounded him. I said, "Yeah, well, okay, I don't mind making a tour for you, but I can't go for no California wages." So he said, "Oh no! We wouldn't go in for that. I'll take care of everything." I said, "Oh you will, huh?" "Yeah." So I said, "Yeah, okay."

So when we went out and made the first week, he gave me two-hundred-and-fifty dollars. And I said, "You're just taking care of me. Right?" So he said, "Well, I know you've got more expense out here on the road than you have in California." I said, "But who's thinking about California? I was thinking about me, period." But he wouldn't get up off no money. He wouldn't give me no money, man.
But I remember seeing you in Kansas City... When I was
going to school in the Midwest, we went to Kansas City to see Jazz at the Philharmonic. It was you and Flip Phillips and Bill Harris and Hank Jones...
Oh yeah.
I forget... But it was...
Yeah, I didn't have nothin' else to do, so what was I gonna do? Turn down two-hundred-fifty dollars? No.

Going back to California, though, I wanted to talk about maybe what you remembered about that Jazz At The Philharmonic that you were on with Bird and Prez, where you did "I Can't Get Started" and "After You've Gone" and those things. Because Bird and Prez really didn't do that much together, and that was one of the few things they did.

Yeah. Well, at that time it was beautiful, because Bird was playing his heart out and so was Prez. I don't know how this came about, but I think that was made in 1948. I think it was '48 that they made that.
I think it was before that.
It was?
Yeah, I would think so.
Well, let's see. Jazz At The Philharmonic came out when, 1945?
Yeah. And this was probably when Bird was still in
California.
Yeah. Well, he came out there with Dizzy, you know.
And then the time with you and...
Yeah.
So I think that's when it was made. Because later he toured for Norman on Jazz at the Philharmonic, but this was...
When they did "Lady Be Good" and shit, that was bad! That was cut in '46.
"Lady Be Good," "I Can't Get Started," right. Al Killian.
Yeah, that's probably '46.
Willie Smith, yourself, Bird and Prez.

Yeah. I felt sorry for everybody after Bird got through playing. I said, "Pshew!" Because Al Killian and Willie Smith and them didn't know what Bird was playing. They didn't have the slightest idea. When Bird got through with it, I said, "Damn, man!" Because Prez didn't want to follow him. Prez followed him, man. Yeah, Prez followed him, but nobody wanted to follow him! Ha. And Willie Smith and those guys... If I was him, I would have said, "No, you've got it, man! You go ahead and play the tune. I don't need to play." Because really, he wasn't talking
about nothing when he got to whining on that saxophone. Because Charlie Parker was playing that son-of-a-bitch.
Let's see, that was made in '46. But we did... We never knew when Norman was making these...
I think he taped most of... Not taped in those days...
Yeah, he had them taped or taped them. Because he did the one here at Carnegie Hall!
They cut them on disks, I think.
Well, no, I think they were taping them.
Well, whatever it was, I think most concerts he got down. Most of the time...
Well, even the first one, the first Jazz At The Philharmonic was put on tape. That wasn't for no disk.
No?

No. That was on tape. I was trying to make a point... I made seven dates with him, and I never knew when he was (?), because he had those machines running back there, and you never knew what was going on. There wasn't no disks being made, though. That much I knew. Because I was checkin' that shit out. I said, "Well, I'll see what's happening so I can put my demands in front." But it must have been on tape, because there wasn't no disks being made.
Asch told me that Norman brought in a tape for him to hear, and that's why he was interested in putting it out --
because he heard the whole thing, you know. And you couldn't do that with no disk. You couldn't put all that on a disk. It had to be on a tape.
Well, in this whole period, of course, you said you came back to New York with Bird, but you started doing your own thing then...
You mean after I left Bird?
Yeah, and you both came back East in '47.
Yeah.
You had already, of course, recorded for Dial. Isn't that about the time you put your own group together?
Yeah. Well, I had my own group together before that.
But I mean again.

Well, I didn't desert the band. I just came out East because I wanted to see Fats, and I wanted to come to New York anyway just to see what the scene was like. So that's why I came here after we played Chicago. I didn't have no job here; I just came here to hang out and to see what the scene was like.

After that I had to go back and join... Norman called me and asked me would I do the Detroit thing, because he figured he could draw a lot of people there because I'm from Detroit, and most of the cats there knew me and they knew I

was from Detroit, so they would come in to see me. That's what he thought. So he had my picture on the front page of the paper and everything. So that's what made his nut for him. But I was on my way back to California, but I had to stop in Chicago, because I had an important engagement there and...
Did you play at the Argyle with your own band?
Not then.
It was not that much later.

Yeah, it was later on, but not right at that time. At that time, I was just going through Chicago, because like I said, I had a hot date, but it was only just... It wasn't for Norman or nobody; it just was for a gig.

And I went on back out to California, and I formed a band, and I stayed out there until the Fall of the year -- that's when I had to come back with Norman and do a tour with Norman. And I came back here to New York... No, I moved back here to New York; that's right.
When was the band that recorded for Dial, with...
You mean here, with Moody and them? That was done here. That was after '47; it was '48 or something like that.
Didn't that band travel all over?
Yeah, I took the band to Chicago..
That's right. A friend of mine had heard that band in Chicago and told me about it.
Well, we had been to Chicago with the group. That was at the Argyle, I think.
Moody had left Dizzy?
Well, I recorded with Moody here.
But wasn't he in the band when you were at the Argyle?
No.
He didn't go to Chicago with you.

No, he didn't go to Chicago. I had Little Jimmy Heath with me. Jimmy and Percy and Milt Jackson and Jeff Davis and Joe Harris, the drummer -- and myself. And a guy named Willie Smith, a little tenor player; he was from California, too.
And Jimmy was playing alto then.
Yeah, Jimmy was playing the alto. We did a few dates out in California when we did that Savoy thing that they call "Maggie..." You've seen that one; that two-album thing.
Mmm-hmm.
We did those dates out in Chicago. But that's later than '47. Well, I guess it was in '47 that we did those dates. Because I went to Paris in...
In '48, the Spring of '48.
With that band? With Vernon Biddle and the Heath Brothers.

Yeah. Well, they were working with me steady, you know. We came here and played up in Utica, and around New York and Philadelphia, and even went down to Baltimore, Washington... Then we played this (?) in Baltimore... Anyway, we did a lot of dates around... I went into the Three Deuces here with that band, with Little Jimmy Heath and Milt...
I think I was in the Midwest at the time. I was going to school, so I didn't hear that band.
It was a good band. It was a real good band.

Something you and I talked about on the other tape we did was the way a musician would get ripped off by record companies, and you were talking about on the Jazz At The Philharmonic you always wanted to know whether he was recording or not so you could protect yourself. Yeah.
You were doing a Jazz at the Auditorium, and you didn't know you were being recorded?
No, you didn't know that they had recorded you. And the next thing you know, you hear yourself playing.

Yeah, on Black-and-White and Modern Records. When they put it out on Modern, I called Jules. I said, "Jules, what are you doing, putting out that album? I didn't get paid for that, you know." I said, "Well, I paid the man." I said, "Well, he didn't pay me." I said, "It's on your label, that's all I know, and you're responsible for it." So he went to the union, and the union made him pay.
But Ralph Bass, and there was another guy there, Gene Norman... That's the one. Gene Norman was another...
He's the one who sold the things to Modern.
Yeah, he's...
Ralph Bass was on Black-and-White.
That's right. You got it straight.
Sure, because all those things came out on Modern with you and Wardell and Erroll Garner...

Anyway, Jules was responsible for the guys getting their money, regardless of who gave him the material. You don't get our(?) material unless you pay for it. But Gene Norman was the guy. I had to threaten him. I told him, "If you don't send me my money, I'm going to get

my attorney on you and I'll tell him to collect it for me. And he'll collect it, put his fees on top of it, and then you will really have to pay somebody." So he got scared behind that, and he hurried up and sent me my money, and the next morning I had a telegram... He sent me one hundred and seventy-five bucks, I believe.
Well, they got a lot of mileage out of those records anyway, because later they were put out on LP...
Yeah. About two or three different companies had them damn things.
Right before that, or in the same period, after the record ban was over, so many new companies cropped up. You did some things for that...
Recording-wise?
Yeah.
See, I recorded for anybody and everybody that had a label.
What was that thing with Willie Smith and Lucky Thompson...?
Laguna's date.
Eddie Laguna?
Yeah. He was one of the ones I got, too. Ha-ha! I mean, I made him give me what I wanted.
Sunset, that was the name of the label.

Yeah, the Sunset label. Yeah, they were giving everybody... They said, "Well, we pay so-and-so-so." I said, "Well, I don't care what you pay them. You pay me such-and-such amount." And that's the only way I could get any money out of the deal! If I had to go along with their program, they'd hand me scale and say, "Yeah, thanks," and shit, they ain't givin' you nothing! You got to speak up for yourself, or else you don't get nothin'.
And wasn't there a thing with Al Benson in Chicago that you told me about?

Yeah, Al Benson got to me, too. But I mean, he was slick. He waited til I left Chicago, and I didn't know about it... Acoustic Records. I had recorded for them, but I didn't know they was goin' out of business. So they didn't pay me for the date, and Al Benson got the masters because I wasn't there to protest against it. Because they owed me money... And he couldn't have got them if I had been in Chicago at the time telling the judge, "Well, Judge, they owe me for this."
So it should have reverted to me.

To me, yeah. And it would have come back to me, you know. But Al Benson said, "Oh, well, he owes me money," so he got the record. And the next thing I know is that they're on the market, and he sold them to somebody
else, and somebody else did it or something. Anyway, they got me; I didn't get paid for those things.

Oh yeah, yeah.
What happened? Was that with strings?
No.

No, it was just a band...

A small group.

No, it wasn't a big band.

What do you mean what happened to them?

Yeah, I got some here -- if I can find them.
I know I got 'em on tape here somewhere.

"Stardust," "Mop-Mop," "Intersection," and I'm trying to think of the fourth title. But whatever, we can look it up later. But those are something I never really heard correctly. And what I heard, I liked, but it was just not... It was off-center.
Well, that's because they didn't know how to record too well out there, you know.
Well, this is more the pressing, I think, than the recording.

Well, hah, that's one of the problems, too. But they didn't know how to make records out there. That was the country folks. Every time I think about California, I think how lucky I was to escape from there.
Well, that brings up another point. You were talking about prejudice in the South before, and of course we know there was prejudice in the North, too, but it was more subtle...
More subtle, right.
...not as out in the open. But California, as you said, it was Country and it was really very Southwestern.
Yeah, Southwestern-Country. That's what it was.
And you did run into some problems there which I think
are worth talking about.

Yeah, they messed with you. Anybody that don't know what they're doing will be hung... Many a musician... Like Dexter Gordon went back out there, but he didn't know what he was going back into. He thought that because he was Dexter Gordon, he was going to get everything that was coming to him. He got everything that was coming to him, all right. They put him in jail every time he turned around.

That's why I split from out there. I saw what was happening, and I'd say, "Well, gee, I ain't gonna be out here in this mess, playing... Let me get out of here." Because I wasn't doing anything bad, but I mean, what they thought was bad, it would be anything, you know.
Well, you were also married to a White woman.
And that was taboo. Yeah, that was really...
So they were after you for that.

Yeah, they didn't like me for that. But what can you say? You just have to make it. If they don't like you there, split, and go somewhere else! I come here to New York and I ain't had no problems like that, you know. And I've been living with a White woman for as long as I can remember, damn near. Even before... When I was with Andy,
when I first met White girls hanging out, I was cool. You know, we got along good together. I didn't have no animosity towards them.

But boy, they really had it for me out in California, though. And I had all the girls in my... I had five girls that come sit at the table the first night I opened up with Coleman Hawkins out there. They all sat at the table, and all of us there... Me, her...yeah, her...her...her -- five of them. Beautiful girls, too, you know. I said, "Well, now, I'll just stay away here!" I didn't want the world to know what I was doing, you know. So I said to them, "Cool it. I'll get back to you. I'll get to you when you want to (?)." But you can't go along with that.
But the recording out in California was pretty good, so I don't understand how they got off-center. The Sunset records came out good.
Well, some of the Modern records came out good. But these particular ones didn't, for some reason.
Are you sure that was Modern? I think that "Stardust" was on another... Melodisc(?), I think it was.
Maybe it was. I don't know. I thought it was on Modern, but...
No, it was on Melodisk.
Maybe that's why.
Yeah, because...
Because the Modern records like "Mad Hype" and those things, they were all right.
Yeah, they were all right. But the "Stardust" thing came out on Melodisk(?), I think that's what that was.
We'll have to check that out.
Yeah. I got here a tape of that, and it don't sound too good...
